questions.stem: A drug has a half-life of 6 hours. The level is 80 mg/L now. With no more doses, what is the level after 12 hours?
questions.explanation: D is correct: 12 hours is 2 half-lives, so 80 halves to 40, then to 20. A is after only 1 half-life. C is after 3 half-lives. B treats the decline as a fixed 20 mg/L drop rather than halving.

questions.stem: A drug has a half-life of 8 hours. About when does it reach steady state on regular dosing?
questions.explanation: C is correct: steady state takes about 4 to 5 half-lives, and 8 hours times 4 to 5 is 32 to 40 hours. A is 1 half-life. B is 2 half-lives. D is wrong because regular doses do climb and flatten at steady state.

questions.stem: With no more doses, what percent of a drug remains after 3 half-lives?
questions.explanation: C is correct: 100 becomes 50, then 25, then 12.5 after 3 half-lives. A is after 1 half-life. B is after 2. D is wrong because each half-life only halves the level; it takes about 4 to 5 half-lives for the drug to be mostly gone.

questions.stem: When should a drug level be checked after starting regular doses (no loading dose)?
questions.explanation: A is correct: check drug levels at steady state, not after the first dose. B is too early; the level is still climbing. C gives no information about the drug's effect. D is wrong because the level keeps rising until steady state.

questions.stem: A patient's phenytoin dose is raised by a small amount. What is the likely effect on the level?

options.text: A big jump, possibly into toxicity

questions.explanation: B is correct: phenytoin's enzymes get saturated, so a small dose increase can cause a big jump in level. A describes a linear drug. C and D are wrong because a dose increase raises the level.

questions.stem: Which statements about phenytoin are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Doubling the dose simply doubles the level
A small dose increase can cause a big jump in level
Its half-life gets longer at higher levels
Toxicity can show as shaky eyes and stumbling

questions.explanation: A, C, D, and E are correct: phenytoin's enzymes saturate, small increases can cause big jumps, its half-life gets longer at higher levels, and toxicity shows as shaky eyes and stumbling. B describes a linear drug, not phenytoin.

questions.stem: A therapeutic level is needed quickly. Which parameter mainly sets the loading dose?
questions.explanation: C is correct: the loading dose fills the volume of distribution. A, clearance, sets the maintenance dose. B, half-life, sets how long it takes to reach steady state. D adjusts for absorption but does not set the size of the tank to fill.

questions.stem: A pharmacist is planning doses for a new patient. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The maintenance dose depends on clearance
The loading dose depends on clearance
The loading dose depends on volume of distribution
Steady state takes about four to five half-lives
A loading dose shortens the drug's half-life

questions.explanation: A, C, and D are correct: the maintenance dose replaces what clearance removes, the loading dose fills the volume, and steady state takes about four to five half-lives. B is wrong because the loading dose follows volume, not clearance. E is wrong because a loading dose gets the level up faster without changing the half-life.

questions.stem: A drug has a volume of distribution of 0.7 L/kg. For a 70 kg patient with a target level of 10 mg/L, what is the loading dose? (Loading dose = volume x target level.)
questions.explanation: D is correct: 0.7 L/kg x 70 kg = 49 L, and 49 L x 10 mg/L = 490 mg. A forgets to multiply by the target level. C is a tenfold slip. B does not use the volume.

questions.stem: A drug has a very large volume of distribution. What does that mean?

options.text: It stays only in the blood
It spreads into tissues, so a bigger loading dose is needed
It needs a smaller loading dose

questions.explanation: B is correct: a big volume means the drug spreads into tissues, so a bigger loading dose is needed to fill the tank. A describes a small volume. C is the opposite of what a big volume needs. D confuses volume with clearance.
